# Question 1 — Definition of computational imaging

## Summary

**Definition:** Process of **indirect** image formation from raw measurements, using computation-intensive algorithms. It relies on the **co-design** of the acquisition system and the reconstruction algorithm (inseparable).

**Pipeline:**

- Traditional: Optics → Recognizable image → Computation (enhancement)
- Computational: Generalized optics → **Coded representation** → Generalized computation → Final images

**Two fundamental steps:**

1. **Optical encoding** — new optics, sensors, light sources
2. **Computational recovery** — new decoding/reconstruction algorithms

**Three disciplinary pillars:** Mathematics (optimization, ML) · Physics (optics) · Computation (algorithms)

**Mathematical formalism:**
$$y = Ax + n$$
- $y$: raw measurements, $A$: measurement operator (physics), $x$: unknown image, $n$: noise
- **Ill-posed** problem (Hadamard) → requires **regularization** (prior on $x$)

**Key difference vs classical image processing:** computation does not only enhance — it **decodes** a representation that is not directly readable.

**Biological analogy:** mantis shrimp (16 photoreceptor types) — sensor and brain are inseparable.

# Question 3 — Particularities of computational imaging in digital photography

## Summary

**Base constraint:** smartphones = tiny sensors with limited optics → quality comes from **algorithms**, not from optics.

**Key opto-algorithmic co-design techniques:**

- **HDR** — Capture $N$ exposures (under/normal/over) → align + merge + *tone mapping* to cover up to 14 orders of magnitude of dynamic range
- **Night mode / Burst** — ~15 short images → sub-pixel alignment → temporal fusion (accumulate light without motion blur)
- **Multi-sensors** — Fuse wide + standard + tele + ToF → super-resolution, synthetic bokeh, variable depth-of-field in post
- **Coded aperture** — Binary mask in the diaphragm → extract depth + all-in-focus image from a single shot
- **Focal stack** — Fuse images focused at different distances → global sharpness across the scene
- **Hyperspectral imaging** — Dozens to hundreds of spectral bands → identify materials/vegetation/pollutants

**Unifying principle:** optics **encodes** → algorithm **decodes**. The two are co-designed and inseparable.

---

# Question 4 — Particularities of computational imaging in medical imaging

## Summary

**Fundamental characteristic: no modality directly produces a 3D image** → all are intrinsically computational.

**Modalities and physical carriers:**

| Modality | Carrier | Reconstruction |
|----------|---------|----------------|
| Radiography (X-ray) | X-rays (transmission) | Direct projection |
| CT scan | X-rays (multi-angle) | Filtered back-projection / iterative |
| PET / SPECT | Radioactive emission (tracers) | Inverse reconstruction → functional/metabolic info |
| MRI | Hydrogen spin precession | Inverse Fourier transform (k-space) |
| Ultrasound | High-frequency pressure waves | Reflection/backscatter |

**Advanced MRI modalities:** fMRI (BOLD → brain activity) · MRA (vessels) · MRS (metabolites) · CDI (electric currents)

**Nano-MRI:** MRFM (~1 nm), NV-NanoMRI (~0.1 nm), ESR-STM (<0.1 nm) — algorithmic reconstruction from indirect signals.

**Domain constraints:** absolute non-invasiveness · maximal diagnostic accuracy · near-real-time speed · U-Net widely adopted for reconstruction/segmentation/detection.

---

# Question 5 — Particularities of computational imaging in microscopy

## Summary

**Core challenge:** operate at the physical limits of optical resolution (Abbe criterion: $\sim\lambda/(2 \cdot NA) \approx 200$ nm), and sometimes beyond thanks to algorithms.

**Techniques presented by resolution scale:**

| Technique | Resolution | Principle |
|-----------|-----------|----------|
| **SP-STM** | Atomic | Spin-polarized tunnel current → magnetic structures atom-by-atom |
| **nc-AFM** | Atomic | Magnetic exchange forces → surface spins |
| **MRFM** | ~1 nm, range ~100 nm | Nano-mechanical resonator + nano-magnet |
| **NV-NanoMRI** | ~0.1 nm, range ~10 nm | NV defect in diamond = magnetic sensor |
| **ESR-STM** | <0.1 nm, range ~1 nm | Tunnel current = signal |
| **Coherent X-ray imaging** | 5 nm (2D), 10 nm (3D) | Lensless, phase+absorption contrast |
| **Focal stack** | Optical microscopy | Fuse images at multiple focal planes (sharpness via Laplacian) |

**Essential particularity:** the image is **never directly observable** — it is **reconstructed algorithmically** from indirect signals (electrical, mechanical, optical).

# Question 6 — Particularities of computational imaging in astronomy

## Summary

**Fundamental particularity:** telescopes (especially radio telescopes) do **not** directly produce images but **visibilities** (correlations between antenna pairs) → algorithmic reconstruction is required.

**The SKA — paradigmatic case:**

| Instrument | Site | Antennas | Frequencies | Baselines |
|------------|------|----------|-------------|-----------|
| SKA1-Low | Australia (Murchison) | 131,072 dipoles (512 stations × 256) | 50–350 MHz | 65 km |
| SKA1-Mid | South Africa (Karoo) | 197 dishes | 0.35–15.4 GHz | 150 km |

**Data volumes:**
- SKA1-Low: ~7 Tb/s after central processor, ~300 PB/year
- Compute required: ~130 PFlops per instrument

**Computational pipeline:** antennas (encode visibilities) → supercomputers Perth/Cape Town (decode into radio images) = sensor–algorithm co-design at planetary scale.

**Underlying technique:** long-baseline interferometry (VLBI / *aperture synthesis*) — simulates a telescope of diameter equal to the separation of the farthest antennas. Algorithms: CLEAN, Bayesian methods.

**Emblematic example:** first image of a black hole (M87*, 2019, Event Horizon Telescope) — planetary stations + ML-based reconstruction.

**Scientific domains:** GR tests, cosmic dawn, dark matter/energy, SETI, cosmic magnetism.

# Question 7 — Principles of deep optics

## Summary

**Definition:** end-to-end (*end-to-end*) co-optimization of physical optics and a neural network for a final task.

**Two-layer architecture:**

- **Physical layer** — lens / coded mask / diffractive element / freeform phase surface, parameterized in a **differentiable** way
- **Digital layer** — neural network decoder

**Training phase:**

1. Differentiable simulation of image formation (physics model)
2. Loss gradient backpropagated through the network **and** through the optical simulation
3. Lens parameters (surface heights, phase) optimized **simultaneously** with network weights via SGD

**Inference phase:**

1. Optimized lens **manufactured physically** (micro-fabrication, 3D printing)
2. Trained network deployed alongside
3. Both layers run together on real data

**Two interpretations:**
- Optical encoder + electronic decoder
- Hybrid optical–electronic neural network (physical layer = first layers)

**Key principle:** optics no longer needs to output a “pretty” image — it must encode the useful information optimally for the target task. Highly aberrated lenses can outperform “perfect” lenses for some tasks.

**Applications:** extended depth-of-field, 3D from a single image, gaze-contingent displays, direct classification.

# Question 8 — Non-line-of-sight imaging

## Summary

**Definition:** reconstruct an object **hidden behind an obstacle** by exploiting light bounces on diffuse surfaces.

**Physical principle — the 3rd bounce:**
$$\text{Laser} \to \text{visible wall} \to \text{hidden object} \to \text{visible wall} \to \text{sensor}$$
The time difference between the 1st bounce (direct) and the 3rd bounce encodes the **3D position** of the hidden object.

**Experimental setup:**

| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| **Picosecond laser** | Ultra-short pulses ($\sim 10^{-12}$ s) for time resolution |
| **2-axis galvanometer mirror** | Scan the laser over many wall points |
| **Beamsplitter** | Separates emission and return to avoid saturation |
| **SPAD sensor** | Single-photon detector, ~ps time resolution |
| **Occluder** | Hides the object to isolate the 3rd-bounce signal |

**Acquired data:** 3D volume $(x', y', t)$ — not directly interpretable.

**Reconstruction:** algorithms inspired by filtered back-projection (CT) or **Phasor Fields** (treat as spatio-temporal wavefield propagation).

**Main challenge:** the useful signal (3rd bounce) is **10–100× weaker** than the direct signal → fast deconvolution or compressed-sensing-like methods required.

**Applications:** autonomous driving (see around a corner) · rescue (locate behind a wall) · medical endoscopy.

# Question 9 — Parameters of human visual system

## Summary

| Parameter | Key value |
|-----------|-----------|
| **Visual acuity** | ~1 arcminute, 20/20 — maximum in fovea (~180 × 10³ cones/mm²) |
| **Field of view** | 200° horizontal (120° binocular + 40° monocular each side), 135° vertical |
| **Temporal resolution** | ~60 Hz (below → flicker perceived) |
| **Dynamic range** | 5 orders (instantaneous) — 14 orders / 46.5 f-stops (adapted) |
| **Color vision** | 3 cone types: S/M/L — perceptually linear space: **CIE Lab** |
| **Spectral sensitivity** | S cones: 419 nm · M: 531 nm · L: 559 nm · Rods: 496 nm |
| **Accommodation** | 8 cm–∞ at age 16 → 50 cm–∞ at age 50 (presbyopia = lens stiffening) |
| **CSF** | Peak at **4–6 cpd**, limit ~60 cpd, low-frequency falloff (lateral inhibition) |
| **Depth perception** | Stereopsis (vergence + binocular disparity) + monocular cues (accommodation + retinal blur) |

**Important notes:**
- The eye’s superior dynamic range motivates HDR techniques
- The CSF explains the acceptability of JPEG compression (removing high frequencies)
- Binocular vision (~120° central) is crucial for stereopsis

# Question 10 — Structure of the human eye

## Summary

**Eye diameter:** ~24 mm. Optical pipeline: cornea + lens (lenses) · iris (aperture stop) · retina (sensor).

**Anterior structures:**

| Element | Role | Key detail |
|---------|------|-----------|
| **Cornea** | ~70% of refraction | Fixed curvature, does not accommodate |
| **Iris** | Diaphragm | Smooth muscles → pupil 2–8 mm depending on light |
| **Anterior chamber** | Cornea–iris space | Filled with **aqueous humour** (nourishes cornea + lens) |

**Lens — accommodation element:**
- ~30% of refractive power
- Ciliary muscles contracted → zonules relaxed → lens **rounder** (near vision)
- Ciliary muscles relaxed → zonules taut → lens **flatter** (far vision)
- Stiffens with age → **presbyopia**

**Posterior structures:**

| Element | Role |
|---------|------|
| **Vitreous body** | Gel (99% water), maintains shape |
| **Retina** | Photosensitive sensor (photoreceptors) |
| **Fovea** | Center of retina, ~1–2 mm, maximum cone density, high resolution |
| **Optic disc** | Optic nerve exit — **blind spot** (no photoreceptors) |
| **Choroid** | Vascular supply to outer retina |
| **Sclera** | External protection (white layer) |

**Inverted organization:** light crosses ganglion + bipolar neurons **before** reaching photoreceptors.

**Refractive errors:**
- Emmetropia: focus on retina (normal)
- **Myopia**: focus before retina → concave lens
- **Hypermetropia**: focus behind retina → convex lens
- **Astigmatism**: irregular curvature → no single focus → cylindrical lens

# Question 11 — Structure and properties of retina

## Summary

**Three-layer structure** (inner → outer):

1. **Retinal ganglion cells** (RGC) — output neurons → optic nerve
2. **Collector cells** — bipolar (relay) + horizontal (lateral integration) + amacrine (modulation)
3. **Receptor cells** — photoreceptors (rods + cones)

> Note: inverted organization — light crosses layers 1 and 2 before reaching layer 3.

**Rods — scotopic system:**

- ~10⁸; extreme sensitivity (respond to 1 photon via phototransduction cascade × 10⁶)
- Strong convergence → low resolution, no color, peak at 496 nm
- Absent from fovea; maximum at 15–20° eccentricity

**Cones — photopic system:**

- ~10⁷; require high luminance
- Near 1-to-1 wiring in fovea → high resolution
- 3 types: **S** (419 nm) · **M** (531 nm) · **L** (559 nm)

**Retinal ganglion cells (RGC):**

- Encode **luminance differences** (not absolute levels)
- **Center-surround** organization: on-center and off-center
- Two classes: **M** (magnocellular — motion, temporal) and **P** (parvocellular — color, spatial detail)

**Spatial distribution:**

- Fovea: maximum cones, high resolution
- Periphery: dominated by rods (max at 15–20°) → look slightly aside to see a faint star
- Blind spot: optic disc, no photoreceptors

**Optic nerve bandwidth:** insufficient to transmit all raw signals → visual encoding begins in the retina.

---

# Question 12 — Primary visual cortex

## Summary

**Visual pathway to V1:**
$$\text{Retina} \to \text{Optic nerve} \to \text{Optic chiasm} \to \text{LGN} \to \text{V1}$$

- **Optic chiasm:** nasal fibers cross → left visual field processed by right hemisphere (and vice versa)
- **LGN:** 2 magnocellular layers (M cells) + 4 parvocellular layers (P cells) — retinotopic organization preserved

**Three types of cells in V1 (Hubel & Wiesel, Nobel 1981):**

| Type | Receptive field | Function |
|------|------------------|----------|
| **Center-surround** | Circular antagonistic | Continuation of retinal processing |
| **Simple cells** | Elongated, fixed position | **Oriented edge** detectors at a specific position/orientation |
| **Complex cells** | Elongated, position-tolerant | Orientation-selective, but less sensitive to exact location |

**Hypercolumns:** V1 organization encoding simultaneously:
- Eye-of-origin (left/right) → ocular dominance columns
- Preferred orientation → orientation columns
- Retinotopic location → global organization

> Hebb’s rule: *neurons that fire together wire together*

**CSF:** reflects frequency filtering properties of V1 (peak 4–6 cpd, limit ~60 cpd, lateral inhibition at low frequencies).

**Streams beyond V1:**

- **Ventral stream** (V1→V2→V4→TEO→TE): the “**What**” — object recognition, color, texture, identity
- **Dorsal stream** (V1→V2→V3→MT→parietal cortex): the “**Where**” — location, motion

**Impact on AI:** Hubel & Wiesel’s discoveries → neocognitron → CNN.

---

# Question 13 — Network models inspired by human visual system

## Summary

**Two core biological inspirations:**

1. Orientation selectivity in V1 → **SIFT** and **HOG** descriptors (histograms of oriented gradients)
2. Hierarchy of the ventral stream (simple → complex → hypercomplex) → **Neocognitron** → **CNN**

**The Neocognitron (Fukushima):**

- Architecture: input → retina → LGN → S layers (simple) → C layers (complex) → … → “grandmother” cell
- **S layers** ↔ V1 simple cells: local oriented filters, position-specific
- **C layers** ↔ V1 complex cells: spatial pooling, translation invariance
- First network capable of translation-invariant recognition

**LeNet (LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, Haffner — 1998):**

$$\text{Image (28×28)} \to \text{Conv C1 (6 filters)} \to \text{Pool S2} \to \text{Conv C3 (16 filters)} \to \text{Pool S4} \to \text{Dense F5 (120)} \to \text{Dense F6 (84)} \to \text{10 classes}$$

- Convolutions = learned Gabor-like filters (good approximation of simple cells)
- Pooling = invariance to small translations (analogy with complex cells)

**Increasing specificity in the hierarchy:**

| Level | Biology (ventral stream) | CNN |
|--------|--------------------------|-----|
| Low | V1: oriented edges (Gabor) | Early layers: edges, colors |
| Mid | V2–V4: combinations, shapes | Intermediate layers: object parts |
| High | IT: faces, whole objects | Deep layers: abstract representations |

**Limitation of the model:** **feedback** connections in the ventral stream (bidirectional, top-down back to V1) are absent from standard CNNs. Good visual architectures are likely hierarchical and mostly feedforward.

# Question 14 — Conventional photography vs. computational photography

## Summary

**Conventional (decoupled) pipeline:**
$$\text{Real world} \to \text{Standard optics} \to \underbrace{\text{Readable image}}_{\text{already interpretable}} \to \text{Computation (enhancement)} \to \text{Final image}$$

**Computational (coupled) pipeline:**
$$\text{Real world} \to \text{Generalized optics} \to \underbrace{\text{Coded representation}}_{\text{not readable}} \to \text{Computation (decoding)} \to \text{Multiple final outputs}$$

**Comparison table:**

| Criterion | Conventional | Computational |
|----------|--------------|--------------|
| Role of optics | Form a readable image | **Encode** information |
| Role of computation | Enhance an already readable image | **Decode** the coded representation |
| Co-design | Independent | **Mandatory** (sensor ↔ algorithm) |
| Outputs | One 2D image | Multiple (sharp image, depth, views, …) |

**Co-design examples:**

- **CFA mosaic (Bayer):** encodes color pixel-by-pixel → demosaicing reconstructs full RGB
- **Plenoptic camera:** encodes ray direction (microlens array) → computation reconstructs refocused views
- **Coded aperture:** encodes depth in blur (PSF) → computation extracts depth map + all-in-focus image

**Physical trade-offs exceeded:**
- Large aperture ↔ shallow depth of field → coded aperture / focal stack
- Light ↔ sharpness → night mode (burst photography)
- Pinhole (everything sharp, little light) ↔ lens (efficient, limited DoF) → computation aims to combine the advantages

---

# Question 15 — Focal stack imaging

## Summary

**Definition:** series of images captured at different focus distances, fused to produce an **all-in-focus** image.

**Analogy:** as HDR extends dynamic range by combining several exposures, a focal stack extends depth of field by combining several focus settings.

**Capturing the stack:**

- Vary $D'$ (lens–sensor distance) via the **focus ring**
- Or vary $D$ (object–lens distance) via **camera/object motion** (macro, motorized rail StackShot)

**3-step fusion:**

1. **Alignment** — correct magnification changes $m = f / (D' - f)$ via isotropic scaling
2. **Sharpness measure** — apply the **Laplacian operator** to each image (strong response = sharp regions) + Gaussian smoothing of weight maps
3. **Weighted fusion** — $I_{\text{sharp}} = \dfrac{\sum_k w_k \cdot I_k}{\sum_k w_k}$ where $w_k$ = sharpness map

**Typical applications:** macro photography (very small DoF) · optical microscopy (DoF ~ µm) · landscape photography.

**Bonus:** the focal stack also enables **depth inference** — the focus setting where a pixel is sharpest reveals its distance to the camera (→ Question 16).

---

# Question 16 — Depth inference technique

## Summary

**Common physical principle:** the size and shape of the **PSF** (*Point Spread Function*) are linked to depth — on-focus → point-like PSF; off-focus → growing circle of confusion.

**Four techniques compared:**

| Technique | Input | Output | Particularities |
|-----------|--------|--------|----------------|
| **Confocal stereo** | Focus **+** aperture stack (2D) | Per **pixel** | Very accurate, resolves depth/texture ambiguity; data-hungry [Hassinof & Kutulakos, ECCV 2006] |
| **Depth from focus** | 1D focal stack | Per **patch** | Standard; Laplacian sharpness, depth = best-focus setting of the patch |
| **Focal flow** | Dense focal stack | Per **patch** | No convolution; models PSF as Gaussian ($\sigma$ varies), measures **optical flow** between frames; works only in textured regions; inspired by the **jumping spider** [Alexander et al., ECCV 2016; Guo et al., ICCV 2017] |
| **Depth from defocus** | **2 images** only | Per **patch** | Minimal data; $g_i = f * h_{\sigma_i}$, compare the two to extract $\sigma$ → depth |

**Key trade-off:** depth accuracy ↔ amount of required data.

---

# Question 17 — Light field photography: main principles

## Summary

**Motivation:** classical photography captures a 2D projection (intensity only) → ray direction lost → focus, aperture, viewpoint fixed at capture.

**Light field:** geometric distribution of light rays in space.

**Plenoptic function:**
- Full version: $L(x, y, z, \theta, \phi)$ — **5D**
- Reduced (free space, radiance conserved along a ray): **4D** via **two-plane parameterization** $(s, t, u, v)$
  - **st** plane = main lens (which microlens)
  - **uv** plane = sensor (which pixel under the microlens)

**Three post-capture numerical operations:**

| Operation | Mechanism | Effect |
|-----------|----------|-------|
| **Stopping down** | Sum only central pixels under each microlens | Increases depth of field |
| **Viewpoint change** | Shift the pixel-extraction window | Creates numerical parallax |
| **Digital refocusing** | Sum shifted windows across neighboring microlenses | Simulates a new focal plane |

**Fundamental trade-off:** total sensor resolution is shared between **spatial** and **angular** resolution (more views → fewer pixels per view).

**Historical origin:** Gabriel **Lippmann** (1908) — *integral photography*, *Scientific American* article of **Aug 19, 1911**.

---

# Question 18 — Light field photography: hardware particularities

## Summary

**Three hardware approaches:**

| Approach | Example | Advantage | Drawback |
|----------|---------|----------|----------|
| **Camera array** | Stanford Camera Array | Simultaneous capture, dynamic scenes | Expensive, complex calibration |
| **Moving single camera** | Camera on a LEGO motor | Low cost, no calibration | Requires a **static** scene |
| **Plenoptic camera** | Lytro | One shot, portable | Reduced spatial resolution |

**Biological analogy (camera array):** insect compound eye — each **ommatidium** captures a different direction.

**Plenoptic camera architecture:**

$$\text{Subject} \to \text{Main lens} \to \underbrace{\text{Microlens array (MLA)}}_{\text{"ray sorter"}} \to \text{Sensor}$$

Each microlens images the aperture onto its pixel group → each pixel encodes **a precise angular direction**.

**Lytro — first commercial realization:**

| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| Lens Array | MLA directly on the sensor |
| Light Field Sensor | CMOS + microlenses |
| Light Field Engine | Dedicated signal processor |
| Marvell Avastar 88W8787 SoC | WiFi + Bluetooth transfer |

**Resolution trade-off:** if each microlens covers $N \times N$ pixels → angular resolution = $N^2$ directions, spatial resolution divided by $N^2$ relative to a conventional camera.

# Question 19 — Imaging with coded apertures

## Summary

**Principle:** insert a **pseudo-random binary mask** in the aperture plane → turn the defocus PSF into a **unique identifier** that is discriminable from naturally smooth image content.

**Basic physical model:**
$$y' = f_k \otimes x$$
where $y'$ = observed image, $x$ = unknown sharp scene, $f_k$ = PSF at depth $k$. Estimating $k$ means finding the $f_k$ that best explains the observation.

**Two challenges with a standard aperture:**

1. Smooth circular PSF is **indistinguishable** from naturally uniform content
2. Deconvolution is **ill-posed** — zeros in the PSF spectrum → lost frequencies + ringing artifacts

**Solution 1 — Prior on natural images:**

Natural images have **sparse gradients** (flat regions + sharp edges) → regularization:
$$x = \arg\min_x \left\| f \otimes x - y \right\|^2 + \lambda \sum_i \rho(\nabla x_i)$$

- $\rho(\nabla x) = \|\nabla x\|^2$ → Gaussian prior (smooth, not ideal)
- $\rho(\nabla x) = \|\nabla x\|^{0.8}$ → **sparse prior** (sharp edges + flat regions, better than Richardson–Lucy)

**Solution 2 — Coded aperture:**

- Binary mask → PSF carries the **mask signature** → identifiable at all depths
- Each depth = scaled version of the pattern → **scale reveals depth**
- Optimal combination: mask with zero frequencies (better discrimination) + sparse prior (stabilizes deconvolution despite zeros)

**Result from a single image:** depth map + all-in-focus image.

**Summary table:**

| | Advantage | Limitation |
|-|---------|------------|
| Input | Single image | — |
| Resolution | No spatial loss | — |
| Hardware | Only a mask in the diaphragm | — |
| Depth | — | Coarse; textureless regions problematic |
| Light | — | Slight loss (mask blocks some rays) |

---

# Question 20 — Imaging with generalized optics

## Summary

**Principle:** modify **the lens itself** (not just the aperture) to encode more information in the measurement.

**Technique 1 — Wavefront coding:**

- Modify the lens surface to introduce a controlled **cubic phase aberration**
- Result: PSF **approximately depth-invariant** over a range
- Digital processing: a **single global deconvolution** restores sharpness over the whole scene
- ✅ Large effective depth of field
- ❌ No depth map (PSFs identical → no depth information)

**Technique 2 — Lattice lens:**

- 2D array of microlenses with **varying focal lengths** placed **in front of** the main lens
  - ≠ plenoptic camera (MLA between lens and sensor)
- PSF **varies with depth** → depth estimation possible
- ✅ Produces depth + sharp image · ✅ Exploits the **dimensionality gap**
- ❌ Requires local patch-wise deconvolution

**Dimensionality gap (Ng, 2005):**

- Full light field: **4D**
- Useful information for image + depth: **3D** (2D image + 1D depth)
- The lattice lens captures precisely this **3D subspace** → more efficient than capturing the full 4D light field when the goal is depth.

**Course-wide recap table:**

| System | Modification | Main advantage | Limitation |
|--------|-------------|----------------|------------|
| Conventional | None | Simplicity | Limited depth of field |
| Focal stack | None (multiple shots) | Sharp image + depth | Static scene |
| Plenoptic camera | MLA between lens and sensor | Refocusing, multi-views | Reduced spatial resolution |
| Coded aperture | Mask in the diaphragm | Depth + sharp image in 1 shot | Coarse depth |
| Wavefront coding | Lens with cubic phase | Large depth of field | No depth map |
| Lattice lens | MLA in front of the lens | Efficient depth + sharpness | Local deconvolution |
